Fiber
A low-fiber diet is often prescribed for patients with narrowed sections of bowel to decrease the 
possibility of intestinal obstruction, minimize physical irritation to the inflamed bowel, reduce 
stool weight and frequency, and slow the rate of intestinal transit. The diet consists of white bread 
and refined cereals and avoidance of high-fiber fresh fruits and vegetables, nuts, skins, and seeds. 
The benefit of a low-fiber diet in managing symptoms or affecting the course of IBD remains 
unclear. Diets should be recommended based on a patient’s individual tolerance and intolerance; 
intake of fiber-rich, nutrient-dense foods can generally be encouraged in the absence of bowel 
strictures and if there is no discomfort. A fiber rich diet should not be prescribed in patients with 
strictures (Crohn’s disease), as this could potentially contribute to a small bowel obstruction.
Fat
Decreased fat intake may help control the symptoms of steatorrhea, especially in patients with 
Crohn’s disease involving the small bowel. However, fats serve as a form of concentrated calories, 
which are needed to promote weight gain in underweight or malnourished patients. Dietary fats 
are also essential for the absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K. In order to decrease diarrhea related
